standing_assumptions: Setting. The work is a textbook: Aronow and Miller, Foundations of Agnostic Statistics (Cambridge University Press, 2019). Every statement is about random variables on a probability space; Part II adds i.i.d. sampling; Part III adds the missing-data and potential-outcomes models. Locations give the printed page and the one-based page of main.pdf (316 pp.; in the body, PDF page = printed page + 18). Statements were transcribed from the page images (the 110 dpi staged renders, with higher-resolution renders of the same PDF pages where subscripts were small) and compared with the text layer for wording. (S1) Probability space. [Definition 1.1.1, p. 6 (PDF p. 24)] A set $S$ of subsets of $\Omega$ is an event space if it satisfies the following: Nonempty: $S \ne \emptyset$. Closed under complements: if $A \in S$, then $A^C \in S$. Closed under countable unions: if $A_1, A_2, A_3, ... \in S$, then $A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup ... \in S$. [Definition 1.1.2, p. 7 (PDF p. 25)] Kolmogorov Axioms. Let $\Omega$ be a sample space, $S$ be an event space, and $P$ be a probability measure. Then $(\Omega, S, P)$ is a probability space if it satisfies the following: Non-negativity: $\forall A \in S$, $P(A) \ge 0$, where $P(A)$ is finite and real. Unitarity: $P(\Omega) = 1$. Countable additivity: if $A_1, A_2, A_3, ... \in S$ are pairwise disjoint, then $P(A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup ...) = P(A_1) + P(A_2) + P(A_3) + ... = \sum_i P(A_i)$. [Footnote 11, p. 8 (PDF p. 26)] This assumption [that $(\Omega, S, P)$ is a probability space] shall henceforth be implicit in all definitions and theorems referring to $\Omega$, $S$, and/or $P$. (S2) Random variables and their distributions. [Definition 1.2.1, p. 16 (PDF p. 34)] A random variable is a function $X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ such that, $\forall r \in \mathbb{R}$, $\{\omega \in \Omega : X(\omega) \le r\} \in S$. [Definition 1.2.2, p. 16] Let $g : U \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function, where $X(\Omega) \subseteq U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. Then, if $g \circ X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ is a random variable, we say that $g$ is a function of $X$, and write $g(X)$ to denote the random variable $g \circ X$. [p. 17 (PDF p. 35)] we use $\Pr[\cdot]$ to denote the probability that some condition(s) on a random variable will hold, or, equivalently, the probability that the event defined by those conditions will occur. [Definition 1.2.4, p. 18 (PDF p. 36)] A random variable $X$ is discrete if its range, $X(\Omega)$, is a countable set. [Definition 1.2.5, p. 18] For a discrete random variable $X$, the probability mass function of $X$ is $f(x) = \Pr[X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.11, p. 21 (PDF p. 39)] For a random variable $X$, the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is $F(x) = \Pr[X \le x]$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.14, p. 24 (PDF p. 42)] A random variable $X$ is continuous if there exists a non-negative function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that the CDF of $X$ is $F(x) = \Pr[X \le x] = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f(u)du$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. The function $f$ is called the probability density function (PDF). [Definition 1.2.15, p. 25 (PDF p. 43), as printed; see finding P001-C01-E002] For a continuous random variable $X$ with CDF $F$, the probability density function of $X$ is $f(x) = \left.\frac{dF(u)}{du}\right|_{u=x}$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.20, p. 31 (PDF p. 49)] For a random variable $X$ with PMF/PDF $f$, the support of $X$ is $\mathrm{Supp}[X] = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : f(x) > 0\}$. [Definition 1.3.1, p. 31] Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. Then $X = Y$ if, $\forall\omega \in \Omega$, $X(\omega) = Y(\omega)$. [Definition 1.3.16, p. 38 (PDF p. 56)] Let $X$ and $Y$ be either two discrete random variables with joint PMF $f$ or two jointly continuous random variables with joint PDF $f$. Then $X$ and $Y$ are independent if, $\forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}$, $f(x, y) = f_X(x)f_Y(y)$. We write $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y$. [Definition 1.4.1, p. 39 (PDF p. 57)] A random vector (of length $K$) is a function $\mathbf{X} : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^K$ such that, $\forall\omega \in \Omega$, $\mathbf{X}(\omega) = (X_{[1]}(\omega), X_{[2]}(\omega), ..., X_{[K]}(\omega))$, where $\forall k \in \{1, 2, ..., K\}$, $X_{[k]}$ is a random variable. (S3) Expectations. [Definition 2.1.1, p. 45 (PDF p. 63)] For a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function (PMF) $f$, if $\sum_x |x|f(x) < \infty$, then the expected value of $X$ is $\mathrm{E}[X] = \sum_x xf(x)$. For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function (PDF) $f$, if $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |x|f(x)dx < \infty$, then the expected value of $X$ is $\mathrm{E}[X] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} xf(x)dx$. [Footnote 2, p. 45] This regularity condition (and the corresponding one in the continuous case) is known as absolute convergence. It is virtually always satisfied in practice, so we omit this technical condition from all subsequent discussion of expectations. [Footnote 3, p. 49 (PDF p. 67)] This theorem, and every subsequent theorem that we only prove for these two cases [two discrete random variables with joint PMF, or two jointly continuous random variables with joint PDF], also holds when one random variable is discrete and the other continuous. [Definition 2.1.12, p. 52 (PDF p. 70)] The variance of a random variable $X$ is $\mathrm{V}[X] = \mathrm{E}[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])^2]$. [Definition 2.1.15, p. 53 (PDF p. 71)] The standard deviation of a random variable $X$ is $\sigma[X] = \sqrt{\mathrm{V}[X]}$. [Definition 2.1.22, p. 57 (PDF p. 75)] For a random variable $X$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$, the mean squared error of $X$ about $c$ is $\mathrm{E}[(X - c)^2]$. [Definition 2.2.1, p. 59 (PDF p. 77)] The covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is $\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y] = \mathrm{E}[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])(Y - \mathrm{E}[Y])]$. [Definition 2.2.5, p. 62 (PDF p. 80)] The correlation of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ with $\sigma[X] > 0$ and $\sigma[Y] > 0$ is $\rho[X, Y] = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y]}{\sigma[X]\sigma[Y]}$. [Definition 2.2.10, p. 67 (PDF p. 85)] For discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PMF $f$, the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = \sum_y yf_{Y|X}(y|x)$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. For jointly continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PDF $f$, the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} yf_{Y|X}(y|x)dy$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [Definition 2.2.12, p. 68 (PDF p. 86)] For random variables $X$ and $Y$, the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{V}[Y|X = x] = \mathrm{E}[(Y - \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x])^2|X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [Definition 2.2.15, p. 69 (PDF p. 87)] For random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PMF/PDF $f$, the conditional expectation function of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $G_Y(x) = \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [p. 70 (PDF p. 88)] We write $\mathrm{E}[Y|X]$ to denote $G_Y(X)$; the conditional variance function is $H_Y(x) = \mathrm{V}[Y|X = x]$, and $\mathrm{V}[Y|X]$ denotes the random variable $H_Y(X)$. [Footnote 14, p. 70] Ignoring some unimportant measure-theoretic regularity conditions, namely $X(\Omega) = \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. The multivariate versions are Definitions 2.3.3 and 2.3.4 (p. 85, PDF p. 103) and the multivariate BLP, Definition 2.3.6 (p. 86, PDF p. 104; transcribed in the targets that use it). (S4) Sampling and asymptotics. [Definition 3.1.1, p. 92 (PDF p. 110)] Let $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ be random variables with CDFs $F_1, F_2, ..., F_n$, respectively. Let $F_A$ denote the joint CDF of the random variables with indices in the set $A$. Then $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ are independent and identically distributed if they satisfy the following: Mutually independent: $\forall A \subseteq \{1, 2, ..., n\}$, $\forall(x_1, x_2, ..., x_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $F_A((x_i)_{i \in A}) = \prod_{i \in A} F_i(x_i)$. Identically distributed: $\forall i, j \in \{1, 2, ..., n\}$ and $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$, $F_i(x) = F_j(x)$. [p. 92] When we have i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, we use the unsubscripted letter $X$ to denote the random variable whose distribution the i.i.d. draws all share. So, for example, $\mathrm{E}[X]$ denotes the expected value common to $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, that is, $\mathrm{E}[X] = \mathrm{E}[X_1] = \mathrm{E}[X_2] = ... = \mathrm{E}[X_n]$. [Definition 3.2.1, p. 96 (PDF p. 114)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, a sample statistic is a function of $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$: $T_{(n)} = h_{(n)}(X_1, X_2, ..., X_n)$, where $h_{(n)} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$, $\forall n \in \mathbb{N}$. [Definition 3.2.2, p. 97 (PDF p. 115)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, the sample mean is $\overline{X} = \frac{X_1 + X_2 + ... + X_n}{n} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i$. [Definition 3.2.6, p. 99 (PDF p. 117)] Let $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be a sequence of random variables and let $c \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $T_{(n)}$ converges in probability to $c$ if, $\forall\epsilon > 0$, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr[|T_{(n)} - c| \ge \epsilon] = 0$, or equivalently, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr[|T_{(n)} - c| < \epsilon] = 1$; written $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{p} c$. [Definition 3.2.22, p. 108 (PDF p. 126)] Let $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be a sequence of random variables with CDFs $(F_{(1)}, F_{(2)}, F_{(3)}, ...)$, and let $T$ be a random variable with CDF $F$. Then $T_{(n)}$ converges in distribution to $T$ if, $\forall t \in \mathbb{R}$ at which $F$ is continuous, $\lim_{n \to \infty} F_{(n)}(t) = F(t)$; written $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{d} T$. [Definition 3.2.28, p. 112 (PDF p. 130)] An estimator $\hat\theta$ is asymptotically normal if $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \phi^2)$, for some finite $\phi > 0$. [Definition 3.3.1, p. 116 (PDF p. 134)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, the empirical CDF $\hat F$ of $X$ is $\hat F(x) = \overline{\mathrm{I}(X \le x)}$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 3.3.2, p. 118 (PDF p. 136)] A statistical functional is a function $T : \mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathcal{F}$ is the set of all possible CDFs. [Definition 3.3.3, p. 118] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ with common CDF $F$, the plug-in estimator of $\theta = T(F)$ is $\hat\theta = T(\hat F)$. The 'usual plug-in regularity conditions' (p. 120, PDF p. 138) are not formally defined in the book (footnote 31 names Hadamard differentiability with respect to the Kolmogorov distance and gives no formal definition). (S5) Regression. [Definition 4.1.2, pp. 146–147 (PDF pp. 164–165), with the plus sign before the last term supplied] For i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), (Y_2, \mathbf{X}_2), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$, the ordinary least squares (OLS) regression estimator is the function $\hat g(\mathbf{X}) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1X_{[1]} + \hat\beta_2X_{[2]} + ... + \hat\beta_KX_{[K]}$ such that $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1, ..., \hat\beta_K) = \arg\min_{(b_0, b_1, ..., b_K) \in \mathbb{R}^{K+1}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(Y_i - (b_0 + b_1X_{[1]i} + b_2X_{[2]i} + ... + b_KX_{[K]i})\right)^2$. We refer to $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ as the OLS coefficient estimator. [Definition 4.1.3, p. 148 (PDF p. 166)] the regressor matrix $\mathbb{X}$ is the $n \times (K + 1)$ matrix whose $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ row is $(1, X_{[1]i}, X_{[2]i}, \cdots, X_{[K]i})$. (S6) Parametric models. [Definition 5.1.1, pp. 178–179 (PDF pp. 196–197)] For a random variable $Y$ and random vector $\mathbf{X}$ of length $K$, a parametric model is a set of functions $g : \mathbb{R}^{K+1} \to \mathbb{R}$ indexed by a real-valued parameter vector $\boldsymbol\theta$ of length $\tau$: $\{g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta) : \boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta\}$, where $\boldsymbol\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^\tau$. The set $\boldsymbol\Theta$ is called the parameter space. The model is said to be true if $\exists\boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta$ such that $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$. [Definition 5.2.1, p. 186 (PDF p. 204)] the likelihood function is $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y, \mathbf{X}) = g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})$, and for i.i.d. observations $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. [Definition 5.2.2, pp. 186–187 (PDF pp. 204–205)] the maximum likelihood estimator of $\boldsymbol\theta$ is $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. (S7) Missing data. [Definition 6.1.1, pp. 208–209 (PDF pp. 226–227)] For an outcome variable $Y_i$, the stable outcomes model is $Y_i^* = -99$ if $R_i = 0$ and $Y_i$ if $R_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$, where $Y_i^*$ is the censored version of $Y_i$ and $R_i$ is an indicator for whether $Y_i$ is observed for unit $i$. [Footnote 2, p. 208] Since we are assuming i.i.d. sampling, our inferences do not depend on the unit subscript $i$. [Definition 6.1.5, p. 213 (PDF p. 231)] $Y_i$ is missing completely at random if $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i$ and $\Pr[R_i = 1] > 0$. [Definition 6.1.8, p. 215 (PDF p. 233)] $Y_i$ is missing at random conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ and $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] > \epsilon$. [Footnote 6, p. 215] For random variables $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ with joint PMF/PDF $f(x, y, z)$, $Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z|X$ if, $\forall y, z \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$, $f_{(Y,Z)|X}((y, z)|x) = f_{Y|X}(y|x)f_{Z|X}(z|x)$. [Definition 6.1.11, p. 217 (PDF p. 235)] the response propensity function is $p_R(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. (S8) Causal inference. [Definition 7.1.1, p. 236 (PDF p. 254)] For an outcome variable $Y_i$ and binary treatment variable $D_i$, the potential outcomes model is $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$, where $Y_i(0)$ denotes the potential outcome under control for unit $i$, and $Y_i(1)$ denotes the potential outcome under treatment for unit $i$. [Definition 7.1.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 255)] $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$. [Definition 7.1.3, p. 238 (PDF p. 256)] the average treatment effect (ATE) is $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$. [Definition 7.1.9, p. 244 (PDF p. 262)] $D_i$ is randomly assigned if $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i$ and $0 < \Pr[D_i = 1] < 1$. [Definition 7.1.12, p. 247 (PDF p. 265)] $D_i$ is strongly ignorable conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ and $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\epsilon < \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] < 1 - \epsilon$. [Definition 7.1.15, p. 250 (PDF p. 268)] the treatment propensity function is $p_D(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. Notes for the formalizer. (a) The book works with PMFs and PDFs and states pointwise conditions ('for all $x$'); for continuous variables these hold only up to null sets (finding P001-C01-E002), so a measure-theoretic formalization should read densities and conditional expectations as versions. (b) Existence and finiteness of the expectations in a statement is a standing convention (footnote 2, p. 45). (c) Asymptotic statements are about an infinite i.i.d. sequence and $n \to \infty$. (d) In a target's statement, text in square brackets is a label or a remark of the transcriber, not the book's words.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Example 7.2.2 (Causal Inference with OLS Regression), the two imputation tables as printed (unit 3 with $X_{[1]i} = 9$) against the claim that both imputations give the same estimate
canonical_claim.location: p. 259 (PDF p. 277), the data table and the two imputation tables
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] Suppose we had the following data: units $1, ..., 6$ with $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1), D_i, X_{[1]i}, X_{[2]i})$ equal to $(?, 2, 1, 1, 7)$, $(5, ?, 0, 8, 2)$, $(?, 3, 1, 10, 3)$, $(?, 10, 1, 3, 1)$, $(?, 2, 1, 5, 2)$, $(0, ?, 0, 7, 0)$. We will start by assuming that, at least to a first approximation, $\mathrm{E}[Y_i|D_i, X_{[1]i}, X_{[2]i}] = \beta_0 + \beta_1D_i + \beta_2X_{[1]i} + \beta_3X_{[2]i}$. Then we could estimate the coefficients with OLS and use the resulting equation to impute the missing values: [first imputation table] unit 1: $Y_i(0) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \cdot 0 + \hat\beta_2 \cdot 1 + \hat\beta_3 \cdot 7$, $Y_i(1) = 2$; unit 2: $Y_i(0) = 5$, $Y_i(1) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \cdot 1 + \hat\beta_2 \cdot 8 + \hat\beta_3 \cdot 2$; unit 3: $Y_i(0) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \cdot 0 + \hat\beta_2 \cdot 9 + \hat\beta_3 \cdot 3$, $Y_i(1) = 3$, with $(D_i, X_{[1]i}, X_{[2]i}) = (1, 9, 3)$; unit 4: $Y_i(0) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \cdot 0 + \hat\beta_2 \cdot 3 + \hat\beta_3 \cdot 1$, $Y_i(1) = 10$; unit 5: $Y_i(0) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \cdot 0 + \hat\beta_2 \cdot 5 + \hat\beta_3 \cdot 2$, $Y_i(1) = 2$; unit 6: $Y_i(0) = 0$, $Y_i(1) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \cdot 1 + \hat\beta_2 \cdot 7 + \hat\beta_3 \cdot 0$. Equivalently, we could instead impute all the potential outcomes, which will yield the same estimate for $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$ and is more straightforward to implement: [second imputation table] for every unit $Y_i(0) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \cdot 0 + \hat\beta_2X_{[1]i} + \hat\beta_3X_{[2]i}$ and $Y_i(1) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \cdot 1 + \hat\beta_2X_{[1]i} + \hat\beta_3X_{[2]i}$, with unit 3 again printed with $\hat\beta_2 \cdot 9$ and covariates $(1, 9, 3)$. In either case, the estimate of $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$ is just the difference-in-means estimator with the imputed values. [What is refuted] That the two imputation tables as printed yield the same estimate, when the coefficients are fitted to the data table (unit 3 with $X_{[1]3} = 10$) and unit 3 is predicted at $X_{[1]3} = 9$ as the two imputation tables print it. The equality with a consistent data set is not refuted. [Calculation, from the validator] OLS of $Y_i$ on $(1, D_i, X_{[1]i}, X_{[2]i})$ with the six observations of the data table ($Y = (2, 5, 3, 10, 2, 0)$, $D = (1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0)$, $X_{[1]} = (1, 8, 10, 3, 5, 7)$, $X_{[2]} = (7, 2, 3, 1, 2, 0)$) gives $(\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1, \hat\beta_2, \hat\beta_3) = \left(\frac{13563}{2437}, \frac{6178}{2437}, -\frac{759}{2437}, -\frac{1778}{2437}\right)$. With unit 3 predicted at $X_{[1]3} = 9$: the first table (impute only the missing potential outcomes) gives the estimate $\frac{12103}{4874}$; the second table (impute all potential outcomes) gives $\hat\beta_1 = \frac{6178}{2437}$. The difference is $\frac{12103}{4874} - \frac{6178}{2437} = -\frac{253}{4874} \ne 0$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the potential outcomes model $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$ (Definition 7.1.1), the unit-level treatment effect $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$ (Definition 7.1.2), the ATE $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$ (Definition 7.1.3); i.i.d. sampling of units; random assignment (Definition 7.1.9); strong ignorability conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ (Definition 7.1.12); the treatment propensity function $p_D$ (Definition 7.1.15); conditional independence (footnote 6, p. 215); expected value, conditional expectation and the Law of Iterated Expectations (Chapter 2). [Definition 7.1.1, p. 236 (PDF p. 254)] Potential Outcomes Model. For an outcome variable $Y_i$ and binary treatment variable $D_i$, the potential outcomes model is $Y_i = Y_i(0)$ if $D_i = 0$ and $Y_i(1)$ if $D_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$, where $Y_i(0)$ denotes the potential outcome under control for unit $i$, and $Y_i(1)$ denotes the potential outcome under treatment for unit $i$. [Definition 7.1.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 255)] the causal effect of treatment for unit $i$ is $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$. [Definition 7.1.3, p. 238 (PDF p. 256)] the average treatment effect (ATE) is $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$. [Definition 7.2.3, p. 260 (PDF p. 278)] Regression Estimator for Causal Inference. Let $Y_i(0)$, $Y_i(1)$, and $D_i$ be random variables with $\mathrm{Supp}[D_i] = \{0, 1\}$. Let $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$ and $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$, and let $\mathbf{X}_i$ be a random vector. Then, given $n$ i.i.d. observations of $(Y_i, D_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$, the regression estimator for $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$ is $\hat{\mathrm{E}}_R[\tau_i] = \hat{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i(1)] - \hat{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i(0)] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i|D_i = 1, \mathbf{X}_i] - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i|D_i = 0, \mathbf{X}_i]$, where $\hat{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i|D_i = d, \mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$ is an estimator of the CEF. [Example 7.2.2, end, p. 260] In the case without interactions or polynomials, the resulting estimate of $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$ is just $\hat\beta_1$. [Theorem 4.1.4, p. 148 (PDF p. 166)] $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\mathbb{X}^T\mathbb{X})^{-1}\mathbb{X}^T\mathbf{Y}$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor (kind: numerical): unit 3's covariate is 10 in the data table and 9 in the two imputation tables (both covariate-column entries and all three factors $\hat\beta_2 \cdot 9$). The example is symbolic and reports no number; the validator's exact fractions show that the typo, executed literally, would break the stated equality. The fractions were recomputed here in exact arithmetic ($\det\mathbb{X}^T\mathbb{X} = 7311 \ne 0$) and agree with the validator's.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Example 7.2.2 (Causal Inference with OLS Regression), unit 3 of the two imputation tables, corrected ($X_{[1]3} = 10$); the two imputations give the same estimate, the OLS coefficient on $D_i$
canonical_claim.location: p. 259 (PDF p. 277); the pooled-regression identity $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i|\mathbf{X}_i] = \beta_1$: p. 258 (PDF p. 276)
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected tables] In unit 3 of the first imputation table: $Y_i(0) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \cdot 0 + \hat\beta_2 \cdot 10 + \hat\beta_3 \cdot 3$, with $(D_i, X_{[1]i}, X_{[2]i}) = (1, 10, 3)$. In unit 3 of the second table: $Y_i(0) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \cdot 0 + \hat\beta_2 \cdot 10 + \hat\beta_3 \cdot 3$, $Y_i(1) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \cdot 1 + \hat\beta_2 \cdot 10 + \hat\beta_3 \cdot 3$, with $(D_i, X_{[1]i}, X_{[2]i}) = (1, 10, 3)$. All other entries as printed. [Statements of the example, as printed] Equivalently, we could instead impute all the potential outcomes, which will yield the same estimate for $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$ and is more straightforward to implement. ... In either case, the estimate of $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$ is just the difference-in-means estimator with the imputed values. [p. 258, population implication with the source hypotheses made explicit] For this population calculation only, let $K\in\mathbb N$, let $\mathbf X_i$ take values in $\mathbb R^K$, let $D_i\in\{0,1\}$ almost surely, and let $Y_i(0),Y_i(1)$ be integrable real potential outcomes with $Y_i=D_iY_i(1)+(1-D_i)Y_i(0)$. Assume strong ignorability conditional on $\mathbf X_i$: $(Y_i(0),Y_i(1))\perp D_i\mid\mathbf X_i$ and there exists $\eta>0$ such that $\eta<p_D(\mathbf X_i)<1-\eta$ almost surely, where $p_D(\mathbf X_i)=\Pr(D_i=1\mid\mathbf X_i)$. Let $\beta_0,\beta_1\in\mathbb R$ and $\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^K$, and assume the displayed linear observed CEF equality exactly (as an almost-sure equality of conditional-mean versions): $\mathrm{E}[Y_i|D_i, \mathbf{X}_i] = \beta_0 + \beta_1D_i + \mathbf{X}_i\boldsymbol\beta$. Then $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i|\mathbf{X}_i] = \mathrm{E}[Y_i|D_i = 1, \mathbf{X}_i] - \mathrm{E}[Y_i|D_i = 0, \mathbf{X}_i] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot 1 + \mathbf{X}_i\boldsymbol\beta - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot 0 + \mathbf{X}_i\boldsymbol\beta) = \beta_1$, so we can estimate the conditional ATE given $\mathbf{X}_i$ using the OLS coefficient estimate $\hat\beta_1$: $\hat{\mathrm{E}}[\tau_i|\mathbf{X}_i] = \hat\beta_1$ ... so we can likewise estimate the ATE with $\hat{\mathrm{E}}[\tau_i] = \hat\beta_1$. The population conclusion is $\mathrm E[Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)\mid\mathbf X_i=x]=\beta_1$ for $P_{\mathbf X_i}$-almost every $x\in\mathbb R^K$, and $\mathrm E[Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)]=\beta_1$. All population conditional equalities in this paragraph are understood up to the corresponding null sets. An unspecified approximation to the linear CEF is not an assumption under which these exact equalities are asserted. The fitted contrast $(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1+x\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})-(\hat\beta_0+x\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})=\hat\beta_1$ is an algebraic identity for every $x\in\mathbb R^K$. [Formal content, finite-sample identities, requiring no causal assumptions] (i) General identity: for any data $(Y_i, D_i, \mathbf{X}_i)_{i=1}^{n}$ with $D_i \in \{0, 1\}$, both arms nonempty, and OLS coefficients $(\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1, \hat{\boldsymbol\beta})$ from the regression of $Y_i$ on $(1, D_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$ with residuals $e_i$: the 'impute all' estimate is $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i\left[(\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 + \mathbf{X}_i\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}) - (\hat\beta_0 + \mathbf{X}_i\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})\right] = \hat\beta_1$; the 'impute only the missing' estimate is $\frac{1}{n}\left[\sum_{i : D_i = 1}(Y_i - \hat\beta_0 - \mathbf{X}_i\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}) + \sum_{i : D_i = 0}(\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 + \mathbf{X}_i\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} - Y_i)\right] = \hat\beta_1 + \frac{1}{n}\left[\sum_{i : D_i = 1} e_i - \sum_{i : D_i = 0} e_i\right] = \hat\beta_1$, because $\sum_i e_i = 0$ and $\sum_i e_iD_i = 0$ (Theorem 4.1.5). (ii) For the six units of the example with $X_{[1]3} = 10$: $(\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1, \hat\beta_2, \hat\beta_3) = \left(\frac{13563}{2437}, \frac{6178}{2437}, -\frac{759}{2437}, -\frac{1778}{2437}\right)$ and both imputation estimates equal $\hat\beta_1 = \frac{6178}{2437}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the potential outcomes model $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$ (Definition 7.1.1), the unit-level treatment effect $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$ (Definition 7.1.2), the ATE $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$ (Definition 7.1.3); i.i.d. sampling of units; random assignment (Definition 7.1.9); strong ignorability conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ (Definition 7.1.12); the treatment propensity function $p_D$ (Definition 7.1.15); conditional independence (footnote 6, p. 215); expected value, conditional expectation and the Law of Iterated Expectations (Chapter 2). [Definition 7.1.1, p. 236 (PDF p. 254)] Potential Outcomes Model. For an outcome variable $Y_i$ and binary treatment variable $D_i$, the potential outcomes model is $Y_i = Y_i(0)$ if $D_i = 0$ and $Y_i(1)$ if $D_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$, where $Y_i(0)$ denotes the potential outcome under control for unit $i$, and $Y_i(1)$ denotes the potential outcome under treatment for unit $i$. [Definition 7.1.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 255)] the causal effect of treatment for unit $i$ is $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$. [Definition 7.1.3, p. 238 (PDF p. 256)] the average treatment effect (ATE) is $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$. [Theorem 4.1.5, p. 149 (PDF p. 167)] for OLS residuals, $\overline{e} = 0$ and $\overline{eX_{[k]}} = 0$ for every regressor. [Data table of Example 7.2.2, p. 259] units $1, ..., 6$: $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1), D_i, X_{[1]i}, X_{[2]i}) = (?, 2, 1, 1, 7)$, $(5, ?, 0, 8, 2)$, $(?, 3, 1, 10, 3)$, $(?, 10, 1, 3, 1)$, $(?, 2, 1, 5, 2)$, $(0, ?, 0, 7, 0)$; observed outcomes $Y = (2, 5, 3, 10, 2, 0)$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor. The corrected example is exact finite arithmetic and an exact algebraic identity. It is the formal content of the part of headline claim P001-ch07-H7 that says that in the pooled linear case the estimate is the coefficient on $D_i$, which held up. The validator notes that changing the data table's 10 to 9 consistently would also give a valid example, but the data table and its later reuse (Example 7.2.4, p. 262) support keeping 10. The numbers in (ii) were recomputed here.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 7.2.3, the maximum likelihood plug-in estimator of $\mathrm{E}[Y_i(d)]$, corrected: the fitted conditional mean evaluated at the observed covariates $\mathbf{X}_i$
canonical_claim.location: p. 261 (PDF p. 279), last display on the page; the population identity above it on the same page
canonical_claim.statement: [Population identity, p. 261, as printed] Suppose that we have strong ignorability and further suppose that we have a parametric model that is true: $g(y, (d, \mathbf{x}), \boldsymbol\theta) = f_{Y_i|(D_i, \mathbf{X}_i)}(y|(d, \mathbf{x}))$. Then it is the case that all average potential outcomes over the support of $D_i$ are point identified, and can be written in terms of the parametric model. The average potential outcome when $D_i = d$ is $\mathrm{E}[Y_i(d)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\mathrm{E}[Y_i|D_i = d, \mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]f_{\mathbf{X}_i}(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x} = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} yg(y, (d, \mathbf{x}), \boldsymbol\theta)dy\right)f_{\mathbf{X}_i}(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x}$, where the first equality holds due to ignorability, and the second holds due to proper specification of the parametric model. [Printed estimator] ... the maximum likelihood plug-in estimator for $\mathrm{E}[Y_i(d)]$ is computed by substituting $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML}$ for $\boldsymbol\theta$ and replacing the expected value with respect to $\mathbf{X}_i$ with a sample mean: $\hat{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i(d)] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} yg(y, (d, \mathbf{x}), \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML})dy\right)$. [Corrected estimator] $\hat{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i(d)] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} yg(y, (d, \mathbf{X}_i), \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML})dy\right)$. [Formal content] (i) Population identity: if $D_i$ is strongly ignorable conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ and $f_{Y_i|(D_i, \mathbf{X}_i)}(y|(d, \mathbf{x})) = g(y, (d, \mathbf{x}), \boldsymbol\theta)$, then $\mathrm{E}[Y_i(d)] = \mathrm{E}\left[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} yg(y, (d, \mathbf{X}_i), \boldsymbol\theta)dy\right]$ for $d \in \{0, 1\}$. (ii) The corrected estimator is the sample mean over $i$ of $\mu(d, \mathbf{X}_i; \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML})$, where $\mu(d, \mathbf{x}; \mathbf{t}) = \int yg(y, (d, \mathbf{x}), \mathbf{t})dy$; the printed summand $\mu(d, \mathbf{x}; \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML})$ does not depend on $i$, so the printed expression equals $\mu(d, \mathbf{x}; \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML})$, the fitted conditional mean at a free value $\mathbf{x}$, not an estimate of $\mathrm{E}[Y_i(d)]$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the potential outcomes model $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$ (Definition 7.1.1), the unit-level treatment effect $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$ (Definition 7.1.2), the ATE $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$ (Definition 7.1.3); i.i.d. sampling of units; random assignment (Definition 7.1.9); strong ignorability conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ (Definition 7.1.12); the treatment propensity function $p_D$ (Definition 7.1.15); conditional independence (footnote 6, p. 215); expected value, conditional expectation and the Law of Iterated Expectations (Chapter 2). [Definition 7.1.1, p. 236 (PDF p. 254)] Potential Outcomes Model. For an outcome variable $Y_i$ and binary treatment variable $D_i$, the potential outcomes model is $Y_i = Y_i(0)$ if $D_i = 0$ and $Y_i(1)$ if $D_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$, where $Y_i(0)$ denotes the potential outcome under control for unit $i$, and $Y_i(1)$ denotes the potential outcome under treatment for unit $i$. [Definition 7.1.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 255)] the causal effect of treatment for unit $i$ is $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$. [Definition 7.1.3, p. 238 (PDF p. 256)] the average treatment effect (ATE) is $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$. [Definition 7.1.12, p. 247 (PDF p. 265)] Strong Ignorability. Let $Y_i(0)$, $Y_i(1)$, and $D_i$ be random variables with $\mathrm{Supp}[D_i] = \{0, 1\}$. Let $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$. Then $D_i$ is strongly ignorable conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if the following conditions hold: $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ (conditional independence assumption); $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\epsilon < \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] < 1 - \epsilon$ (positivity). [Definition 5.2.10, pp. 197–198 (PDF pp. 215–216)] the ML plug-in estimator $\hat\psi_{ML} = T(\hat F_{ML})$. [p. 262 (PDF p. 280)] The ML plug-in estimator for $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$ is therefore given by $\hat{\mathrm{E}}_{ML}[\tau_i] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} yg(y, (1, \mathbf{X}_i), \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML})dy - \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} yg(y, (0, \mathbf{X}_i), \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML})dy\right)$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor (kind: notation): a lower-case $\mathbf{x}$ is printed for $\mathbf{X}_i$ in the last display of p. 261; the preceding sentence ('replacing the expected value with respect to $\mathbf{X}_i$ with a sample mean') and the next display give the intended average over the observed covariates. This is a correction to the definition of an estimator; the provable content is the population identity (i), which is Theorem 7.1.13 in integral form for a continuous $\mathbf{X}_i$. The first sentence of the section cites Section 5.2.4 under a wrong title (cross-reference slip P001-C07-N005).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The paragraph after Example 7.2.4 (Propensity Score Matching): the comparison of donors for unit 2, corrected ($P_2$ for $P_1$); with the matching estimate of the example
canonical_claim.location: Example 7.2.4: pp. 262–263 (PDF pp. 280–281). Paragraph after it: pp. 263–264 (PDF pp. 281–282)
canonical_claim.statement: [Example 7.2.4, as printed] Suppose we had the following data: units $1, ..., 6$ with $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1), D_i, X_{[1]i}, X_{[2]i}, p_D(\mathbf{X}_i))$ equal to $(?, 2, 1, 1, 7, 0.33)$, $(5, ?, 0, 8, 2, 0.14)$, $(?, 3, 1, 10, 3, 0.73)$, $(?, 10, 1, 3, 1, 0.35)$, $(?, 2, 1, 5, 2, 0.78)$, $(0, ?, 0, 7, 0, 0.70)$. ... The procedure for (one-to-one, nearest-neighbor) matching is perhaps the simplest possible: for each treated unit, find the control unit that is closest on $p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)$ and use that unit's outcome to fill in the missing control potential outcome for the treated unit. Likewise, for each control unit, find the treated unit that is closest on $p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)$ and use that unit's outcome to fill in the missing treatment potential outcome for the control unit. In this example, this yields [the completed table] $Y_i(0) = 5, 5, 0, 5, 0, 0$ and $Y_i(1) = 2, 2, 3, 10, 2, 3$. So the matching estimate of $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$ is $\frac{22}{6} - \frac{15}{6} = \frac{7}{6} \approx 1.17$. [Printed sentence, pp. 263–264] In the above example, we used $Y_1(1) = 2$ to impute $Y_2(1)$ because $P_1 = 0.33$ is closest to $P_2 = 0.14$. But $P_4 = 0.35$ is almost as close to $P_1$, so $Y_4(1) = 10$ probably also gives us some information about $\mathrm{E}[Y_i(1)|p_D(\mathbf{X}_i) = 0.14]$. [Corrected sentence] ... But $P_4 = 0.35$ is almost as close to $P_2$, so $Y_4(1) = 10$ probably also gives us some information about $\mathrm{E}[Y_i(1)|p_D(\mathbf{X}_i) = 0.14]$. (Here $P_j$ stands for $p_D(\mathbf{X}_j)$.) [Formal content] With the propensity scores of the table, treated units $\{1, 3, 4, 5\}$ and control units $\{2, 6\}$: for control unit 2 ($0.14$) the distances to the treated units are $0.19, 0.59, 0.21, 0.64$, so its nearest treated unit is unit 1 and the second nearest is unit 4, at a distance larger by $0.02$; for control unit 6 ($0.70$) they are $0.37, 0.03, 0.35, 0.08$, so its nearest treated unit is unit 3; for the treated units 1, 3, 4, 5 the distances to control units 2 and 6 are $(0.19, 0.37)$, $(0.59, 0.03)$, $(0.21, 0.35)$, $(0.64, 0.08)$, so their nearest controls are units 2, 6, 2, 6. The imputed values are therefore $Y_1(0) = 5$, $Y_3(0) = 0$, $Y_4(0) = 5$, $Y_5(0) = 0$, $Y_2(1) = 2$, $Y_6(1) = 3$; the means of the completed columns are $\frac{22}{6}$ and $\frac{15}{6}$, and the matching estimate is $\frac{7}{6}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the potential outcomes model (Definition 7.1.1), strong ignorability (Definition 7.1.12), the treatment propensity function $p_D$ (Definition 7.1.15). [Section 7.2.4, p. 262 (PDF p. 280)] one-to-one, nearest-neighbor, with-replacement, propensity score matching; for the moment the propensity scores are assumed known.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor (kind: notation): $P_1$ is printed for $P_2$ in an illustrative sentence, and the shorthand $P_j$ is not introduced; the matching example and its estimate are unaffected. The parallel slip in Chapter 6 is P001-C06-N004. The target records the corrected comparison as exact arithmetic on the example's table and checks the example's estimate $\frac{7}{6}$; it belongs to headline claim P001-ch07-H8 (one-to-one nearest-neighbour propensity score matching).
